body:
## Module 7 in two minutes

Governance is usually taught as values — principles, a fairness statement, a commitment to human oversight. Those documents are sincere and they do nothing, **because a principle has no configuration screen.** This module treats governance as design: every obligation resolves to a tier, a setting, a name, or a signature.

**Three tiers for every decision in your register.** May draft — a system produces a first version a human then owns. May recommend — a system offers, a human chooses. May never touch. And the test that keeps the middle tier honest: **a recommendation only counts as one if declining it is normal.** If your reviewers accept 99%, you have an automated decision with a signature step, and everyone will find that out at the same awkward moment.

The axis that sorts them is neither stakes nor difficulty — both attract supervision precisely because they're frightening. It is: **does this decision require judgment whose absence nobody would notice?** That's where the danger concentrates, because **the failures that matter are the ones where nothing looked wrong.**

And the sentence the module is named for: **the decision that matters most is where to stop — and it's a design decision made in advance, not a value asserted afterwards.**

### Article 26 is mostly settings

Three tracks in this curriculum end their legal module by telling the learner to find out who the deployer is. **For you, it is you** — and that is a statutory allocation, not a rhetorical flourish.

Read as a checklist: use the system per the provider's instructions for use (which requires that somebody read them). **Assign *competent* human oversight — to a person**, with the knowledge and standing to intervene. Manage input data. **Keep logs for at least six months** — a retention period somebody sets in a pane, where the common default of 30 or 90 days is probably already wrong. Monitor, and notify the provider and authority of serious incidents.

And the sentence that ends every procurement argument: **these obligations attach to the deployer and cannot be contracted away.** An indemnity allocates who pays afterwards. It does not move a duty.

**The timing trap.** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 came into force 27 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations — where employment sits — to **2 December 2027**. **Article 50 was not deferred.** Its transparency duties, including telling a person at first contact that they are talking to an AI, became enforceable **2 August 2026**, with penalties to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover — and they catch an organization **with no high-risk AI at all** if it runs a chatbot.

> The deadline your function is watching slipped sixteen months. The one governing your service desk did not.

**The full module adds three more surfaces.** US litigation reaches the same conclusion by another route: in *Mobley v. Workday* the agent theory has let claims proceed on the basis that a vendor screening candidates on your behalf can be your agent. **The agent doctrine and Article 26 say the same thing in two languages — the obligation does not transfer with the invoice.** And state the May 2026 privilege ruling precisely: a motion to compel bias-testing data was denied *because counsel had curated the analysis and used it in giving legal advice.* Not "bias testing is privileged" — **the structure determined the protection, so involve counsel before you test.**

**Co-determination is a dependency, not a message.** German BetrVG §90 requires informing and consulting the works council **at the planning stage**; §80(3) presumes an employer-funded external expert; §95 reaches AI-established selection criteria. A labour court held that merely *permitting* a browser-based AI tool did not trigger co-determination — so the line is what the system does inside your estate. Put consultation on the plan with a duration.

**And four rules collide on your logs**: your retention schedule, Article 26's six months, a legal hold that overrides both, and possible confidential medical information from Module 4's territory. The most valuable thing you can do this quarter is unglamorous — **tell your legal team the system exists and generates records**, because a hold cannot reach a system nobody mentioned.
